L857@P15: Nares Strait, a channel leading NNE from Baffin Bay to
L858@P15: the Arctic Ocean, passes between the W side of the N part
L859@P15: of Greenland and the E coast of Ellesmere Island in Canada.
L860@P15: Nares Strait, from S to N, consists of Smith Sound, Kane
L861@P15: Basin, Kennedy Channel, Hall Basin, and Robeson Channel. The N end of Robeson Channel opens out into a portion
L862@P15: of the Arctic Ocean named the Lincoln Sea. Nares Strait is
L863@P15: about 300 miles long from the S end of Smith Sound to the
L864@P15: N end of Robeson Channel, and varies in width from about
L865@P15: 10 to 25 miles except in Kane Basin, where it opens out
L866@P15: to a width of about 85 miles. Deep water to within a short
L867@P15: distance of the contiguous shores is found throughout the
L868@P15: channels and basins forming the waterway, except on the E
L869@P15: side of Kane Basin.
L870@P15: The land on the W, or Ellesmere Island, coastline rises precipitously from the frozen sea to irregular mountains whose
L871@P15: partly rounded peaks are generally marked by ice caps. Great
L872@P15: glaciers fill the valleys and discharge icebergs into the various bays and fjords. Only the projecting rocky headlands and
L873@P15: some of the lower points in the bays are free of snow and

L3113@P48: The master of a vessel which requires icebreaker assistance should bear in mind that the icebreaker can arrive at
L3114@P48: the position of the vessel within 48 hours of the request to
L3115@P48: the Chief of the Kara Sea Navigation Service, but if in the
L3116@P48: opinion of the Service the ice situation is not of emergency, a
L3117@P48: plane will be sent to investigate the ice zone; the Service will
L3118@P48: then advise the vessel as to how to proceed, without aid, to
L3119@P48: open water, or to move to another area more favorable from
L3120@P48: the point of view of ice conditions.
L3121@P48: The above regulations also apply to vessels proposing to
L3122@P48-49: proceed W from Kara sea. Of the four above routes, the shortest passage from Nordkapp (North Cape) to Ostrov Belyy Pub. 180, The Arctic Ocean
L3123@P49: 40
L3124@P49: is through Proliv Matochkin Shar, the next shortest through
L3125@P49: Proliv Karskiye Vorota, and the next through Proliv Yugorskiy Shar. If proceeding to Obskaya Guba, the route N of
L3126@P49: Novaya Zemlya is shorter than by Proliv Yugorskiy Shar, and
L3127@P49: if proceeding to the mouth of Reka Yenisey it is even shorter
L3128@P49: than that by Proliv Karskiye Vorota.
L3129@P49: Subject to the above general regulations, when approaching Kara sea, the vessel should determine which of the straits
L3130@P49: is clear of ice and steer for it. The Arkhangel’sk and Proliv
L3131@P49: Matochkin Shar radio stations transmit data of the ice observations of the Kara Hydrometeorological Stations daily,
L3132@P49: to which will be added, during the navigational season, particulars of the ice, which will be communicated to vessels in
L3133@P49: Kara sea at the same.
L3134@P49: Due to the limited range of visibility, the observations of
L3135@P49: the Kara stations only give the ice conditions in their vicinity. If, for example, Yugorskiy Shar and Vaygach report the
L3136@P49: absence of ice in the straits and at sea on the horizon, this does
L3137@P49: not always signify that there is no ice at all near the straits; for
L3138@P49: the edge of the ice may be from 15 to 20 miles from the entrance to them, having been borne away by the tidal currents
L3139@P49: and the wind. Therefore, before finally selecting the route
L3140@P49: for passing into Kara sea, the observations of the stations for
L3141@P49: several days previously should be studied. A sharp drop in
L3142@P49: the temperature of the surface water at the stations with the
L3143@P49: wind blowing from the sea; fog remaining on the horizon at
L3144@P49: sea; the prevalence of winds from the direction in which the
L3145@P49: ice may be moving; all this taken together may help to give
L3146@P49: a good idea of the ice conditions.
L3147@P49: Should a vessel have no information concerning the ice
L3148@P49: except that sent by the radio stations, it should proceed to
L3149@P49: Proliv Yugorskiy Shar or Proliv Karskiye Vorota, preferably
L3150@P49: the former; if these straits are closed by ice or the ice is concentrated immediately E of them, it should proceed to Proliv
L3151@P49: Matochkin Shar, provided the latter is not ice bound or the
L3152@P49: observatory cannot see any ice at sea.
L3153@P49: If all the straits are clear of ice, but the state of the ice
L3154@P49: beyond is unknown, at the beginning of navigation it is best
L3155@P49: for the vessel to make for the S straits, since the ice E of them
L3156@P49: is usually weaker in structure and more passable than on the
L3157@P49: parallel of Proliv Matochkin Shar. The route through Proliv
L3158@P49: Karskiye Vorota should only be selected in preference to that
L3159@P49: through Proliv Yugorskiy Shar when it is quite certain that
L3160@P49: there is no ice farther E or that it is open and easy to pass
L3161@P49: through; usually, if the ice remains NE of Proliv Yugorskiy
L3162@P49: Shar, it is also E of Proliv Karskiye Vorota.
L3163@P49: If the ice conditions in the SW part of the Kara Sea and E of
L3164@P49: Proliv Matochkin Shar are unfavorable, it is sometimes possible and even easier to proceed round the N end of Novaya
L3165@P49: Zemlya. There have been years when the routes through all
L3166@P49: the straits or E of them, as well as round the N end of Novaya
L3167@P49: Zemlya, have been closed by ice.

L3503@P52: The Barents Sea is bordered on the S by the coasts of N
L3504@P52: Norway and Russia, on the W and N by the archipelagos
L3505@P52: of Svalbard and Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa, respectively, and on
L3506@P52: the E by Novaya Zemlya and Ostrov Vaygach. It adjoins the
L3507@P52: Norwegian Sea between Norway and Svalbard, and the Kara
L3508@P52: Sea between Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa and Novaya Zemlya.
L3509@P52: The SW part of the Barents Sea is kept from freezing by the
L3510@P52: comparatively warm water of the North Cape Current, thus
L3511@P52: permitting year round navigation. The remainder of the sea
L3512@P52: is encumbered with ice during part or all of the year.
L3513@P52: The mainland coast of the Barents Sea is rocky and indented by numerous fjords in the W, and is low in the E. The
L3514@P52: S part of the Barents Sea cuts deeply inland to form a large
L3515@P52: body of water known as Beloye More (White Sea).
L3516@P52: Barents Sea covers an area of 1,424,000 km2
L3517@P52:  with a volume of 316,000 km3
L3518@P52: . The greatest depths are in the W part
L3519@P52-53: of the sea. At this location a trough with the greatest depth Pub. 180, The Arctic Ocean
L3520@P53: 44
L3521@P53: of 600m (within the Barents Sea) enters the Norwegian Sea.
L3522@P53: The Barent Sea is characterized by extensive shallow areas
L3523@P53: where banks are crossed by gutters. The rugged bottom relief
L3524@P53: of the Barents Sea has a significant effect on its hydrology.
L3525@P53: The position of the Barents Sea in the high latitudes goes
L3526@P53: beyond the Polar circle, and its connection with the Atlantic
L3527@P53: Ocean and Central Arctic Basin dictate the main climatic
L3528@P53: feature. The water circulation in the Barents Sea is generally
L3529@P53: counterclockwise. Yet, inflows from the neighboring basins
L3530@P53: and the rugged bottom relief cause a complicated system of
L3531@P53: currents to be formed. The E part of Barents Sea is entirely
L3532@P53: on the continental shelf. Depths vary from 100 to 350m with
L3533@P53: complicated bottom topography resulting from glacial action, producing many gentle rises and depressions. Bottom

L3582@P53: The Beaufort Sea
L3583@P53: The Beaufort Sea forms a part of the Arctic Ocean and is
L3584@P53: a wedge shaped area bounded, on the S, by the N coasts of
L3585@P53: Alaska and Canada and, on the E, by the most westerly of
L3586@P53: the islands of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.
L3587@P53: The N limit of the Beaufort Sea is a line extended from
L3588@P53: Point Barrow, the N point of Alaska, then leading to Lands
L3589@P53: End (76°22'N., 122°36'W.) on Prince Patrick Island.
L3590@P53: The E limit is formed by the coast of Prince Patrick Island

L3809@P55: East Siberian Sea
L3810@P55: The East Siberian Sea, lying between Ostrov Vrangelya
L3811@P55: and Novosibirskiye Ostrova, about 100 miles NE, is a shallow basin that deepens gradually NE from gently sloping
L3812@P55: shores. The depths along the shore and within the East Siberian Sea vary considerably.
L3813@P55: The W part of the sea, S of Novosibirskiye Ostrova, and
L3814@P55: the waters along its S shore as far E as the approaches of the
L3815@P55: Reka Kolyma are shallow with numerous shoals.
L3816@P55: The central and E parts of the East Siberian Sea and the
L3817@P55: waters adjacent to the coast are deeper and clear of known
L3818@P55: dangers. Except for Ostrova Medvezh’i, which lie N of the
L3819@P55: mouth of the Reka Kolyma between about 19 miles NE and
L3820@P55: 58 miles E of Mys Krestovyy, the islands off the coast are
L3821@P55-56: few and close to shore. Pub. 180, The Arctic Ocean
L3822@P56: 47
L3823@P56: To the E of Novo Sibirskiye Ostrova, the shelf remains
L3824@P56: wide, but the continental slope becomes less steep than that
L3825@P56: bordering the Laptevykh Sea. The East Siberian Sea is very
L3826@P56: shallow, with depths of 10 to 20m in the W and 30 to 40m
L3827@P56: in the E.
L3828@P56: In shallow water, the seabed consists mainly of sandy silt
L3829@P56: with pebbles and broken boulders. In deeper water, nearer
L3830@P56: the shelf edge, mud predominates.
L3831@P56: In the W area of the East Siberian Sea, W of the Reka
L3832@P56: Kolyma (161°E.), ice conditions are practically always favorable during the navigational period, unless a spell of onshore winds drives the ice back towards the coast. The E area
L3833@P56: of the East Siberian Sea, E of the Reka Kolyma, is the most
L3834@P56: difficult part of the Northern Sea Route, with the exception
L3835@P56: of the region of Proliv Borisa Vil’kitskogo.
L3836@P56: The vegetation along the shores of the East Siberian Sea
L3837@P56: is uniform but poor. Except where there are rocky outcrops,
L3838@P56: there is the usual Arctic covering of tundra. The tundra is
L3839@P56: hummocky and in places patchy; in most places it is marshy
L3840@P56: and is covered, sometimes fairly dense with grass. Creeping
L3841@P56: willows and dwarf birches are found in a few places, and
L3842@P56: in the more elevated and drier parts there is reindeer moss.
L3843@P56: A variety of flowering plants bloom during the short Arctic
L3844@P56: summer in places sheltered from the wind.
L3845@P56: The Kara Sea
L3846@P56: The Kara Sea is located on the E of the Novaya Zemlya,
L3847@P56: N of the Polar circle. It is bounded on the S by the N coast
L3848@P56: of Siberia; on the W by Ostrov Vaygach, Novaya Zemlya,
L3849@P56: and a line drawn from the NE extremity of Novaya Zemlya
L3850@P56: to the E extremity of Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa; on the E by a
L3851@P56: line drawn from the E extremity of Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa to
L3852@P56: the N extremity of Severnaya Zemlya; and on the E by the
L3853@P56: W coasts of Severnaya Zemlya.
L3854@P56: In addition to adjoining the Barents Sea between Novaya
L3855@P56: Zemlya and Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa, the Kara Sea is connected
L3856@P56: with it by Proliv Yugorskiy Shar, between the mainland and
L3857@P56: Ostrov Vaygach; by Proliv Karskiye Vorota, between Ostrov
L3858@P56: Vaygach and Novaya Zemlya; and by Proliv Matochkin Shar,
L3859@P56: which divides Novaya Zemlya into two islands.
L3860@P56: The E part of the Kara Sea is connected with the Laptev
L3861@P56: Sea by Proliv Borisa Vil’kitskogo, Proliv Shokal’skogo, and
L3862@P56: Proliv Krasnoy Armii. The greater part of the Kara Sea is
L3863@P56: covered with ice throughout the year. The most favorable ice
L3864@P56: conditions during the navigation season are found in the region where the large Siberian rivers, bringing comparatively
L3865@P56: warm water, flow into the sea. Detailed exploration in the
L3866@P56: eastern part of the Kara Sea, formerly rendered impracticable
L3867@P56: by the constant ice, has in recent years been facilitated by the
L3868@P56: use of icebreakers and aircraft. A number of islands front the
L3869@P56: S shore of the Kara Sea, and several outlying islands are in
L3870@P56: the N and NE parts of the sea.
L3871@P56: The sea covers an area of 993,000 km2, having a volume
L3872@P56: of 101,000 km3
L3873@P56: .
L3874@P56: The Kara Sea has a diversified bottom relief; the average depth is 113m with the greatest depth being 620m. Its
L3875@P56: S and E parts are shallow, as 40 percent of the area is less
L3876@P56: than 50m deep. Only 2 percent of the sea area is deeper than
L3877@P56: 500m. The Kara shelf is divided N to S by two troughs, the
L3878@P56: St. Ann trough and Voronin. Along the E coast there are the
L3879@P56: Novaya Zemlya and Eastern-Novozemelal’sky troughs, with
L3880@P56: depths of 200 to 400m. The Kara Sea and the Barents Seas are
L3881@P56: connected by Yugorsky Shar, Kara Gate, and the Matochkin
L3882@P56: Shar. In the N part, the seas are connected by a broad passage
L3883@P56: between the Npoint of Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land.
L3884@P56: The Kara Sea is mostly shallow to medium depth and entirely on the continental shelf; in it are two areas of deeper
L3885@P56: water: A deep (600m) N to S rift which starts at the N end of
L3886@P56: Novaya Zemlya and runs N to the E of Zemlya Frantsa Iosifa;
L3887@P56: and the Novaya Zemlya Trough (300 to 400m), which lies
L3888@P56: close E of Novaya Zemlya.
L3889@P56: Elsewhere, the Kara Sea is occupied by a series of platforms or broad terraces stepping down from the SE to N and
L3890@P56: W, where the continental slope edge lies at about 200m.
L3891@P56: The seabed consists mainly of clay and mud in the shallower areas, with mud predominating in the deeper waters.
L3892@P56: The counterclockwise current eddy favors the accumulation
L3893@P56: of mud at shallow depth in the SW part of the sea. Shallow deposits near river mouths are made up of sands and silty sands.
L3894@P56: Although the proximity of the Atlantic Ocean makes the
L3895@P56: climatic conditions milder, the climate remains Arctic. The
L3896@P56: Atlatic effect, warm water develop air masses encountering
L3897@P56: the high mountains of Novaya Zemya, as a result making
L3898@P56: the Kara Sea climate more severe than that of the Barents
L3899@P56: Sea. The climatic features of the Kara Sea (monsoon winter
L3900@P56: cooling and summer warm-up) also influence the formation
L3901@P56: of hydrological conditions of the sea.
L3902@P56: Runoff from the Ob and Yenisey rivers influences the Kara
L3903@P56: Sea hydrology. The Kara Sea receives 1,290 km3
L3904@P56:  of river
L3905@P56: waters annually. The Ob river discharges 450 km3
L3906@P56:  and the
L3907@P56: Yenisey about 600 km3. The Ob-Yenisey runoff causes a significant circulation in the Kara Sea.
L3908@P56: On all the shores of the Kara Sea, the vegetation is poor
L3909@P56: and of a characteristic Arctic nature. In most places there is a
L3910@P56: covering of tundra, but in parts of Novaya Zemlya there are
L3911@P56: outcrops of sedimentary slate; in the W part of Poluostrov
L3912@P56: Taymyrskiy there are outcrops of gneisso-granite, and parts
L3913@P56: of N Novaya Zemlya and of Severnaya Zemlya are covered
L3914@P56: by glaciers. The tundra is lumpy and is covered with grass,
L3915@P56: which is sometimes thick as, for instance, in Poluostrov Yamal. In most places the tundra is marshy and in some places
L3916@P56: it is patchy. Here and there the ground is covered with creeping willow or dwarf birches. Iceland moss is sometimes seen
L3917@P56: in the higher, drier and sandy places. Many species of wild
L3918@P56: flowers grow in places sheltered from the wind and bloom
L3919@P56: in masses during the short Arctic summer.
L3920@P56: Huge flocks of geese migrate to breed during the summer
L3921@P56: in the Kara Sea region. During the moulting season, which
L3922@P56: occurs about the end of July or beginning of August, these
L3923@P56: birds are unable to fly and are killed in large numbers. Besides
L3924@P56: geese there are ducks (including the eider duck in Novaya
L3925@P56: Zemlya), loons and several species of snipe and gulls. The
L3926@P56: arctic owl is a resident. Eagles, gerfalcons and hawks are
L3927@P56-57: found on the mainland coast and on Ostrov Vaygach. Bird Pub. 180, The Arctic Ocean
L3928@P57: 48
L3929@P57: rookeries, some of great extent, are found in many places
L3930@P57: along the W coasts of Novaya Zemlya.
L3931@P57: The Laptev Sea
L3932@P57: The Laptev Sea lies between Severnaya Zemlya and Novosibirskiye Ostrova and the continental coast continued S.
L3933@P57: It consists of a shallow basin, with shifting off lying shoals
L3934@P57: and banks in the S part. The depths gradually increase to the
L3935@P57: N limit, which is the edge of the continental shelf extending
L3936@P57: SE from the N end of Severnaya Zemlya.
L3937@P57: The meridian of 139°E has been designated by the government of Russia as an arbitrary boundary separating the NE
L3938@P57: part of the Laptev Sea from the adjacent East Siberian Sea.
L3939@P57: The SE part of the Laptev Sea is connected with the East
L3940@P57: Siberian Sea by Proliv Dmitriya Lapteva, Proliv Sannikova,
L3941@P57: and Proliv Eterikan, which are the straits of Novosibirskiye
L3942@P57: Ostrova. The S continental shores of the Laptev Sea are mostly low barren tundra indented by several large gulfs and bays
L3943@P57: into which the principal rivers flow.
L3944@P57: The character of the continental shelf in the Laptev Sea
L3945@P57: differs markedly from that of the Kara Sea. Apart from some
L3946@P57: deep troughs around Severnaya Zemlya, the shelf is very flat
L3947@P57: and, on average, less than 75m in depth. Very shallow zones
L3948@P57: extend beyond the mouths of the large rivers. The shelf is
L3949@P57: narrow, seaward of Severnaya Zemlya, but widens to nearly
L3950@P57: 300m off the NE coast of Siberia. The continental slope begins at 200m and falls steeply to 1,000m. Bottom deposits
L3951@P57: in the shallower areas are mainly sand and mud, but some
